content: A bridging approach could potentially be developed for other chemical groups of pesticides. For pesticide mixtures with a concentration greater than 5%, a default dermal absorption value of 25% is applied. For mixtures with a concentration of 5% or less, a default value of 75% is used, as per EFSA guidelines (2012). In the absence of high-quality data on dermal absorption of dry insecticides deposited on the skin or transferred from surfaces, the higher estimate of the active ingredient (whether concentrated or diluted) is used (EFSA 2011, 2014). An experienced toxicologist should evaluate the range and quality of available human and animal toxicity data. While toxicity tests are useful for assessing the hazard potential of insecticides used in indoor residual spraying, it is important to acknowledge that not all tests may have been performed, and some studies may lack quality. Consequently, the data may only be valid for risk assessment with certain restrictions. Even when high-quality studies are missing for some toxic endpoints, potential health hazards can often be characterized through a weight-of-evidence analysis. Identifying critical data gaps that could introduce uncertainty into the assessment is essential. If the database is poor, information on chemically related compounds may be helpful in the assessment. Additionally, the nature, severity, and reversibility of observed effects, as well as the ability to identify dose-response relationships, no-observed-adverse-effect levels (NOAELs), and lowest-observed-adverse-effect levels (LOAELs), are important. Insecticides that meet the criteria for carcinogenicity, mutagenicity, or reproductive toxicity categories 1A and 1B under the Globally Harmonized System (GHS) of Classification and Labeling of Chemicals are considered highly hazardous pesticides (HHPs) (UN, 2015; JMPM, 2008). When two or more insecticides are used concurrently, potential interactions between them should be considered. Insecticides with similar mechanisms of action may produce additive toxic effects, such as organophosphates reducing acetylcholinesterase activity. For toxicants with dissimilar mechanisms, the combined effect can be estimated using response addition or effect addition methods. Other interactions, such as synergistic (supra-additive) or antagonistic effects, may occur due to metabolic interactions between different classes of insecticides. Interactions may also occur between the active ingredient and solvents in the formulated product, potentially affecting the final toxicity. Dose-response assessment is a critical component of hazard evaluation for deriving health-based guidance values and assessing risks. The standard NOAEL approach identifies a dose level assumed to be without appreciable adverse effects. Alternatively, the benchmark dose (BMD) method calculates a dose at which a specific level of response occurs, providing a more comprehensive analysis of the dose-response curve. For substances with endocrine-mediated toxicity, the shape of the dose-response curve may not be well-defined, complicating risk assessment. For most toxic endpoints, it is generally accepted that there is a dose or concentration below which adverse effects do not occur, allowing for the identification of NOAELs and LOAELs. For non-genotoxic carcinogenicity, critical cancer events may exhibit threshold phenomena. NOAEL and LOAEL values are study-specific and influenced by factors such as study design and test system sensitivity. These values are used as surrogates for true no-effect and lowest-effect levels. The BMD model can serve as an alternative to the NOAEL-based approach when appropriate dose-response data are available. Unlike NOAELs, which represent a single dose level, BMDs utilize data from the entire dose-response curve. BMD models are particularly useful for low-dose extrapolation, such as in genotoxic carcinogenicity, where dose-response is assumed to be linear. Uncertainty factors (UFs) are applied to account for variability and uncertainties in the data when setting tolerable systemic dose (TSD) levels. Default UFs of 10 are typically used for interspecies differences and interindividual variability unless chemical-specific data justify modifications. For example, if chemical-specific toxicokinetic or toxicodynamic data suggest higher variability, UFs should be adjusted accordingly. Acute reference doses (ARfDs) are derived from relevant human or animal studies of acute dosing, using NOAELs and applying UFs. For organophosphates and carbamates, acetylcholinesterase inhibition is an appropriate parameter for setting ARfDs. Groups potentially exposed to insecticides through indoor residual spraying include spray operators and residents (adults, children, and breastfed infants). Additional chemical-specific information can improve the accuracy of risk assessments for these groups. Bioaccumulative active ingredients, such as DDT, require specific data on metabolism and toxicokinetics for accurate risk assessment. Misuse, such as using contaminated clothing or equipment, is difficult to quantify and is not typically covered in risk assessments. Specific cases, such as lactating mothers working as operators, should be considered separately.
